title: Localized graph Jacobian from a prescribed cotangent-fibre basis
statement: Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field], $r,d\geq0$, $n=r+d$ and $P=k[y_1,\ldots,y_n]$ [def-weil-pbc-mv-polynomial-ring]. Fix $F_1,\ldots,F_r\in P$, put $A=P/(F_1,\ldots,F_r)$ and let $a_b$ be the image of $y_b$. Assume this is a standard smooth presentation [def-weil-pbc-standard-smooth-algebra], so the image of $\det(\partial F_a/\partial y_b)_{a,b\leq r}$ is a unit. Let $\mathfrak q\subset A$ be prime and $K=\kappa(\mathfrak q)$ [def-weil-pbc-localization-at-prime]. Fix $H_1,\ldots,H_d\in P$ with images $h_j\in A$ such that $dh_j\otimes1$ is a $K$-basis (a linearly independent spanning family) of $\Omega_{A/k}\otimes_AK$ [def-weil-pbc-kahler-differentials, def-weil-module-base-change]. Put $R=k[T_1,\ldots,T_d]$, acting on $A$ by $T_j\mapsto h_j$. Let $J$ be the $n\times n$ matrix [def-weil-matrix] whose rows are the $y$-partial derivatives of $F_1,\ldots,F_r,H_1-T_1,\ldots,H_d-T_d$ [def-weil-pbc-polynomial-partial-derivative]. Its entries lie in $P$. Set $\Delta=\det J\in P$ [def-weil-pbc-matrix-determinant] and let $\delta\in A$ be its image. Then $\delta\notin\mathfrak q$. More precisely, partition $J$ after its first $r$ rows and columns into the upper-left, upper-right, lower-left and lower-right blocks $B,C,D,E$, respectively and put bars on matrices reduced to $K$. The matrix $\overline B$ is invertible; relative to the basis $da_{r+1}\otimes1,\ldots,da_n\otimes1$, the coefficient rows of $dh_j\otimes1$ form the invertible matrix $S=\overline E-\overline D\overline B^{-1}\overline C$, and $\det\overline J=\det\overline B\det S\ne0$. For the localization $A_\delta$ [def-weil-ring-localization-away], the map $y_b\mapsto a_b/1$, $t\mapsto\delta^{-1}$ induces an isomorphism of $R$-algebras $$R[y_1,\ldots,y_n,t]/(F_1,\ldots,F_r,H_1-T_1,\ldots,H_d-T_d,\Delta t-1)\xrightarrow{\sim}A_\delta.$$ The Jacobian of these $n+1$ equations in $(y_1,\ldots,y_n,t)$ has determinant $\Delta^2$, with unit image $\delta^2$ in $A_\delta$; hence the displayed isomorphism is a square Jacobian presentation [def-exc-jacobian-presentation] for the specified $R$-algebra structure. Empty matrices have determinant $1$, including when $r=0$ or $d=0$.

proof.text: Apply [lem-weil-pbc-standard-smooth-kahler-basis] with base $k$, $c=r$ and the given presentation: $e_i=da_{r+i}$ ($1\leq i\leq d$) is an $A$-basis of $M=\Omega_{A/k}$. Its base-changed vectors are a $K$-basis: explicitly the mutually inverse coordinate maps are $M\otimes_AK\to K^d$, $(\sum_i u_i e_i)\otimes\lambda\mapsto(\overline u_i\lambda)_i$, and $K^d\to M\otimes_AK$, $(\lambda_i)_i\mapsto\sum_i e_i\otimes\lambda_i$. The first is balanced and therefore defined on the tensor; the tensor relations give both composites equal to the identity. This also proves the assertion when $d=0$.

source.place: Tag 00T7 (lemma-standard-smooth), part (2) and first proof paragraph; explicit chosen-coordinate calculation following the blueprint differential criterion.

proof.text: The polynomial differential formula of [lem-weil-pbc-polynomial-ring-kahler-basis] remains valid after evaluation $y_b\mapsto a_b$. Indeed the $k$-derivation $P\to\Omega_{A/k}$ given by $G\mapsto d(G(a))$ induces the $P$-linear map $\Omega_{P/k}\to\Omega_{A/k}$ sending $dy_b$ to $da_b$, by [def-weil-pbc-kahler-differentials]. Apply it to $F_a$ and $H_j$ and tensor with $K$. Writing $u=(da_1\otimes1,\ldots,da_r\otimes1)^t$, $v=(e_1\otimes1,\ldots,e_d\otimes1)^t$ and $w=(dh_1\otimes1,\ldots,dh_d\otimes1)^t$, we obtain $\overline B u+\overline C v=0$ and $w=\overline D u+\overline E v$. The first right-hand side is zero because $F_a(a)=0$.

source.place: Tag 00T7 (lemma-standard-smooth), part (2) and first proof paragraph; explicit chosen-coordinate calculation following the blueprint differential criterion.

proof.text: The determinant formula [def-weil-pbc-matrix-determinant] is a finite sum of products, so it commutes with the maps $P\to A\to K$. Thus $\det\overline B$ is the image of the unit specified by [def-weil-pbc-standard-smooth-algebra] and is a unit of $K$. For $r>0$, [lem-weil-pbc-matrix-adjugate-identity] gives the two-sided inverse $(\det\overline B)^{-1}\operatorname{adj}(\overline B)$; for $r=0$ the empty identity is its own inverse. Multiplying the first relation of Step 2 by this inverse gives $u=-\overline B^{-1}\overline C v$. Substitution into the second gives $w=S v$ with $S=\overline E-\overline D\overline B^{-1}\overline C$. Hence these are exactly the claimed coefficient rows.

source.place: Tag 00T7 (lemma-standard-smooth), part (2) and first proof paragraph; explicit chosen-coordinate calculation following the blueprint differential criterion.

proof.text: Both $v_i$ and $w_j$ are $K$-bases, the former by Step 1 and the latter by hypothesis. Write $v_i=\sum_j Q_{ij}w_j$ using the latter basis. Substituting $w=S v$ and comparing coefficients in the $v$-basis gives $QS=I$; substituting $v=Qw$ and comparing coefficients in the $w$-basis gives $SQ=I$. Thus $S$ is invertible. If $d>0$, determinant multiplicativity in [lem-sfb-matrix-cramer-determinant-identities] gives $\det S\det Q=1$, so $\det S\ne0$. If $d=0$, its determinant is $1$ by [def-weil-pbc-matrix-determinant].

source.place: Tag 00T7 (lemma-standard-smooth), part (2) and first proof paragraph; explicit chosen-coordinate calculation following the blueprint differential criterion.

proof.text: Put $L=\begin{pmatrix}I_r&0\\-\overline D\overline B^{-1}&I_d\end{pmatrix}$. Direct block multiplication gives $L\overline J=\begin{pmatrix}\overline B&\overline C\\0&S\end{pmatrix}$. By [lem-weil-pbc-block-triangular-determinant], $\det L=1$. The same lemma applied to the transpose of the latter matrix gives $\det(L\overline J)=\det\overline B\det S$. Here $\det M^t=\det M$ follows directly from [def-weil-pbc-matrix-determinant]: replace the summation permutation $\sigma$ by $\sigma^{-1}$, reindex the finite product, and use $\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma^{-1})=\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)$. If $n>0$, determinant multiplicativity [lem-sfb-matrix-cramer-determinant-identities] now yields $\det\overline J=\det\overline B\det S\ne0$; if $n=0$, every determinant is $1$. The image of $\delta$ in $K$ is $\det\overline J$, again by the finite determinant formula. If $\delta\in\mathfrak q$, that image would be zero under $A\to A_{\mathfrak q}\to A_{\mathfrak q}/\mathfrak qA_{\mathfrak q}=K$ [def-weil-pbc-localization-at-prime]. Therefore $\delta\notin\mathfrak q$.

source.place: Tag 00T7 (lemma-standard-smooth), part (2) and first proof paragraph; explicit chosen-coordinate calculation following the blueprint differential criterion.

proof.text: Let $C_0$ be the displayed quotient $R[y_1,\ldots,y_n,t]/(F,H-T,\Delta t-1)$. Evaluation $y_b\mapsto a_b/1$, $t\mapsto\delta^{-1}$ and $T_j\mapsto h_j/1$ kills every relation, hence gives an $R$-algebra map $f:C_0\to A_\delta$ by the polynomial evaluation and quotient definitions. Conversely $y_b\mapsto[y_b]$ defines $g:A=P/(F)\to C_0$ because $F_a([y])=0$. It is $R$-linear since $[H_j]=[T_j]$. Moreover $g(\delta)=[\Delta]$ is a unit with inverse $[t]$. By [lem-weil-pbc-localization-away-universal-property], $g$ extends to $\widetilde g:A_\delta\to C_0$. The composite $f\widetilde g$ fixes every $a/1$ and therefore is the identity by that same uniqueness. The other composite fixes $R$ and every $[y_b]$; it fixes $[t]$ because both $\widetilde g(\delta^{-1})$ and $[t]$ are inverses of $[\Delta]$, and inverses are unique. Polynomial evaluation and surjectivity of the quotient map give $\widetilde g f=1$. These maps are therefore the specified isomorphism of $R$-algebras.

source.place: Tag 00T7 (lemma-standard-smooth), part (2) and first proof paragraph; explicit chosen-coordinate calculation following the blueprint differential criterion.

proof.text: Take partial derivatives over $R$ in exactly the ordered variables $(y_1,\ldots,y_n,t)$ and equations $(F_1,\ldots,F_r,H_1-T_1,\ldots,H_d-T_d,\Delta t-1)$. By [def-weil-pbc-polynomial-partial-derivative] the matrix is $\begin{pmatrix}J&0\\ t\,\partial\Delta/\partial y_1\ \cdots\ t\,\partial\Delta/\partial y_n&\Delta\end{pmatrix}$: $T_j$ is a coefficient, the first $n$ equations have no $t$, and $\Delta$ has no $t$. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-block-triangular-determinant] with block sizes $n$ and $1$: the determinant is $(\det J)\Delta=\Delta^2$. Under Step 6 its image is $\delta^2$, a unit with inverse $\delta^{-2}$ in $A_\delta$. There are $n+1$ equations and $n+1$ variables, so the displayed isomorphism is a square Jacobian presentation by [def-exc-jacobian-presentation]. All formulas include empty blocks; if $n=0$ the last equation is $t-1$ and its derivative is $1$.
